data.title: Trump unloads on critics in wide-ranging Thanksgiving Day rant
data.description:
President Trump marked Thanksgiving Day with a lengthy rant on social media in which he lashed out at his political opponents, accused federal officials of releasing “fake” economic numbers and called for the mass expulsion of Somalis from the U.S.

In a grievance-filled post on Truth Social, the president began by wishing Americans a happy Thanksgiving holiday before turning his attention to his call for an investigation into economic data released ahead of the midterm elections.

“I would like to wish a Happy Thanksgiving to even those who issued fake Economic Numbers, just prior to the Election, and corrected them yesterday, three weeks late showing that the GDP was actually 4.3%, versus 3.4%, A RECORD SETTING ERROR, and one so grave that it should be immediately investigated,” Trump wrote.

The Commerce Department’s Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA) said Wednesday that the economy grew at an annualized rate of 4.3 percent between July and September, up from its initial estimate of 3.4 percent.

Trump alleged without evidence that the initial gross domestic product (GDP) estimates were deliberately understated and called for an investigation into the figures earlier Thursday after Republicans lost control of both the House and Senate in a midterm election cycle dominated by voters’ concerns over inflation and the rising cost of living.

GDP estimates are routinely revised as more comprehensive data becomes available. The BEA is scheduled to release another estimate next month.

Trump also accused Democrats and the “Radical Far Left” of seeking to impose Sharia law in the U.S. court system and force Americans to redistribute their money “so that all of the hardworking people that have built up, over a lifetime, a certain Wealth, will now be forced to distribute it throughout the Country, even to those who refuse to work.”

The president then turned his attention the Somali community, claiming without evidence that a fraction of the country’s Somali population works without receiving federal aid.

“I want to thank the 2% of our Somalian population that have a job, and are actually willing to work, without receiving Government Assistance,” he wrote. “These are wonderful American ‘citizens,’ and should be allowed to stay in our Country, and celebrate Thanksgiving with us. The others should be thrown out, immediately.”

Trump has repeatedly disparaged Minnesota’s Somali community amid federal investigations into widespread fraud involving government-funded social services programs in the state.

The president also touted his renovations to the White House, ripping the media and others who have criticized his changes to the complex, including the construction of a massive ballroom in the East Wing.

“I took time out of my very busy schedule to fix the 17 broken windows, numerous chipped and decaying columns, broken, dilapidated, and missing moldings, and lack of a proper plaster and paint job on the White House,” he wrote. “Today, it has never looked better, and will soon have the Ballroom that Presidents have sought for over 150 years.”

data.title: Thanksgiving has a bumpy history
data.description:
Happy Thanksgiving! That holiday greeting may seem nongermane to a Congress blog, but it is not. Just as the contemporary turkey day is practically synonymous with wall-to-wall pigskin games on television, historically the national celebration became something of a political football. Before you squeal and cry foul, let me explain.

From grade school, we are all familiar with the origins of America’s Thanksgiving. The Pilgrims in the Massachusetts Bay colony, having landed on our shores in November1620 after an arduous 66-day voyage across the Atlantic on the Mayflower, were grateful for their safe arrival. In 1621, they invited their indigenous Wampanoag neighbors to join them in a harvest feast of celebration. In 1623, they held a similar celebration after a prolonged drought.

Fast forward to our revolutionary war. The Continental Congress crafted the first national proclamation of thanksgiving in 1777 in their temporary quarters in York, Pa. The draft of the proclamation, penned by Sam Adams, thanked the “Almighty God” for the blessings bestowed upon them and implored him “to smile upon us in the prosecution of a just and necessary war…and to crown our arms with the most signal success.”            

Not to be outdone, Gen. George Washington, leading our revolutionary forces, proclaimed in December 1777 that thanksgiving should be a victory celebration honoring the defeat of the British in the battle of Saratoga.

During its existence from 1774 to 1789, the Continental Congress issued several proclamations designating “national days of prayer, humility, and thanksgiving.” This practice continued under our new government.

Shortly after the first House of Representatives adopted the First Amendment to the Constitution guaranteeing the freedom of speech, the press, and religion in 1789, Rep. Elias Boudinot of New Jersey proposed that the House and Senate request President Washington to proclaim a day of thanksgiving “for the many signal favors of Almighty God.”

Washinton obliged by issuing the first proclamation of Thanksgiving Day by the national government, to be observed on Thursday, Nov. 26, 1789. His successor as president, John Adams, followed suit.

Thomas Jefferson, on the other hand, our third president, refused to issue any proclamation. As a deist, he explained his reasoning in an 1802 letter to the Danbury Baptist Association. He thought that religiously oriented declarations by government violated our First Amendment’s wall separating church and state and its guarantee of the free practice of religion. “Believing that religion is a matter which lies solely between Man and his God,” he wrote, “the legitimate powers of government reach actions only, and not opinions.”    

Jefferson’s successor, James Madison, in 1814, at the end of the War of 1812, resumed the precedent set by Washington and Adams. However, neither of Madison’s two proclamations in 1815 was observed. Instead, states like Massachusetts, New Hampshire, and New York began celebrating their own thanksgiving days on dates of their choosing.

It wasn’t until the middle of the Civil War that President Abraham Lincoln, the first president since Madison’s proclamations, began the regular practice of issuing annual Thanksgiving Proclamations. In 1870, President Ulysses S. Grant signed into law the Holidays Act that designated specific federal holidays in Washington, D.C., including New Year’s, July 4, and Christmas, though Thanksgiving was left to the discretion of the president.

One of the more interesting tugs-of-war over Thanksgiving occurred under President Franklin Roosevelt. With encouragement from Fred Lazarus, Jr., founder of the Federated Department Stores, Roosevelt in 1939 proposed making Thanksgiving the fourth Thursday of November instead of Lincoln’s “final Thursday.” Because it was considered inappropriate to advertise goods for Christmas before Thanksgiving, Roosevelt thought allowing an extra week between the holidays would help lift the economy out of the Great Depression and be a boon to merchants and workers alike. 

On Oct. 6, 1941, the U.S. House of Representatives passed a bill that embraced Lincoln’s final Thursday in November as Thanksgiving. However, two months later, the Senate amended the bill switching the date back to the fourth Thursday. The House, after considerable debate, eventually caved and accepted the Senate amendment. And that’s how it still stands today. 

This whole tempest in a turkey pot had devolved into a partisan hissing match, with Democrats referring to Nov. 30 as the “Republican Thanksgiving,” and Republicans referring to Nov. 23 as the “Democratic Thanksgiving” or “Franksgiving.”

Who would have thought that this day of family gatherings, peace, and gratefulness was once a source of wartime invocations of the Almighty, First Amendment feuds, and partisan pettiness? Be thankful for today’s gridiron clashes.          

Don Wolfensberger is a 28-year congressional staff veteran, culminating as chief-of-staff of the House Rules Committee. He is author of, “Congress and the People: Deliberative Democracy on Trial,” and, “Changing Cultures in Congress: From Fair Play to Power Plays.”

data.title: Zeldin: No airborne lead detected in Iowa a day after Army blast
data.description:
The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) said Thursday that its air monitors have detected no airborne lead following the Army’s controlled detonation of thousands of pounds of unstable explosives in southeastern Iowa, though the agency is still awaiting laboratory results from its environmental testing.

EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin said more than 300 agency employees and contractors have collected over 1,000 samples of air, soil and water since Wednesday’s detonation of nearly 10,000 pounds of lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown.

“EPA’s 4 Xact air monitors have all reported a ZERO DETECT of airborne lead since the mitigated detonation,” Zeldin wrote in a Thursday post on the social platform X.

The agency expects to complete sample collection by the end of Thursday and begin receiving laboratory results as early as Friday.

Vice President Vance praised the agency’s efforts Thursday on social media following Zeldin’s update.

“Amazing job to Lee and the team at EPA. Proud of our team,” Vance wrote.

President Trump similarly touted the initial reports from Iowa on Wednesday, saying the Army’s mitigation efforts had “far exceeded expectations.”

The federal government has maintained that the detonation was necessary to prevent an uncontrolled explosion involving the deteriorating material, which the Army deemed too dangerous to transport. The operation drew scrutiny from residents, public health experts and lawmakers concerned about the potential contamination of surrounding communities and farmland.

Exposure to the toxic metal can damage children’s braids and nervous systems and cause developmental and behavioral problems, according to the EPA.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries ripped the Trump administration over the detonation after accusing officials of failing to adequately address the health risks of detonating five tons of lead munitions.

“The potential fallout could span multiple states and has forced Americans to evacuate their homes the day before Thanksgiving,” Jeffries said Wednesday in a statement.

Federal officials lifted a shelter-in-place order Wednesday evening after declaring the operation a success. In a joint statement, six federal agencies said the detonation successfully eliminated the threat posed by the deteriorating lead azide and said Iowa residents in the affected area could safely resume their normal activities.

data.title: FIFA says 'limited set of personal and business information' stolen in cyber attack
data.description:
FIFA, the international governing body for soccer, said Thursday that it had been subject to a cyberattack that resulted in a “limited set of personal and business information” that was stolen. 

“FIFA can confirm that it has been the victim of a criminal cyber-attack resulting in unauthorised access to a limited set of personal and business information,” the governing body said in a statement to The Hill, adding that it’s convening the appropriate officials to investigate the incident. 

“FIFA condemns in the strongest possible terms the unlawful acquisition and publication of information, particularly personal data,” FIFA said. “Such actions constitute a serious and unacceptable violation of privacy and can have significant consequences for the individuals concerned.” 

Sources who spoke with The Athletic said the cyberattack happened as a result of the hacker or hackers pretending to be staff of the football governing body. A group called the Handsome Boy Hacking Club has claimed to be behind the cyberattack, according to various news outlets, though FIFA did not identify who was behind the move.  

Less than a tenth of a percent of the body’s data was compromised, those sources told The Athletic. BBC reported that a sell-off plan pitched by FIFA President Gianni Infantino, which has since been ditched, was not a part of the data compromised. 

The FBI warned in May that cyber actors were trying to create websites that looked akin to the international soccer governing body’s online domain to collect personal information and sell fake soccer tickets. 

“Spoofed websites may mimic the legitimate URL by using a minor misspelling, such as fiffa[.]com, or alternative top-level domains, such as .org rather than .com,”  the FBI said in an advisory earlier this year. “This form of cyberattack — called typo squatting — relies on Internet users making mistakes, such as common typos, when visiting a URL. Threat actors may also register illegitimate websites such as jobs-fifa[.]com to impersonate legitimate subdomains.” 

“If a threat actor gains access to a victim’s [personal identifiable information], they can create new accounts in a victim’s name and ultimately defraud the victim,” the FBI added.

data.title: New IRS audits of top earners drop sharply: Here's what to know
data.description:
(NewsNation) — Top earners faced far fewer new audits over the past year, a drop the IRS partly attributes to its focus on more complex cases with potentially higher payoffs.

In fiscal 2026, the IRS started 2,153 audits of individuals with $10 million or more in positive income, down about 42% from the year before and slightly below its target, according to the agency’s annual financial report.

The latest tally is about half the 2023 total, when new audits of top earners hit 4,326, though roughly in line with the 2021 level.

In the report, the IRS said it prioritized “higher-yield, more complex examinations” that could improve tax compliance, which contributed to the decline among high earners.

The drop follows a Biden-era push to boost IRS enforcement funding, but Congress has since rescinded much of that. The IRS’ audit staff has shrunk from roughly 15,300 in fiscal 2024 to about 10,500 in January 2026, according to a Treasury watchdog.

But experts caution that the story isn’t as simple as the IRS focusing less attention on high earners. That’s because new audits of partnerships and large corporations have risen over the past year, and high earners’ income can be tied to them.

New audits of large corporations, those with at least $250 million in assets, rose 44% to 2,140 in fiscal 2026, the highest total in at least five years. New partnership audits were up nearly 13% from the year prior, though still below the recent peak in 2023.

“It is hard to disentangle enforcement directed at partnerships from enforcement directed at wealthy individuals,” Jeff Hoopes, an accounting professor at the University of North Carolina, said in an email, noting that one partnership audit can potentially affect many high-income individuals.

Max Risch, an assistant professor at Carnegie Mellon University’s Tepper School of Business, said the report’s figures are consistent with a shift toward more complex audits.

“These audits are harder, they take more time, they take more resources, but the return on them could be greater,” he said.

Hoopes added that fewer audits don’t necessarily mean less effective enforcement, and said it’s not clear the IRS should be doing more high-income audits.

“I think there is an argument for the IRS to be auditing where the cost per additional dollar of tax revenue is lowest, and that may not be high-income individuals,” he wrote.

Total IRS enforcement revenue rose to $96.8 billion in fiscal 2026, up from $93.8 billion the year before, according to the report. In its discussion of the results, the IRS said it expanded its use of “advanced analytics,” which help it identify higher-risk cases and prioritize enforcement resources.

The report doesn’t say how much of the enforcement revenue came directly from audits. The Treasury Inspector General for Tax Administration found audits brought in about 7% of enforcement revenue in fiscal 2025, while most came from collection efforts.

It’s unclear how many of this year’s new audits have closed or how much money the IRS has collected from them so far. Large corporate audits can take several years to finish, according to the agency’s budget documents.

The IRS declined to comment when NewsNation contacted it.

data.title: Stop chasing billionaires — fix the broken corporate tax system instead
data.description:
The defeat of California’s billionaire asset tax proposal earlier this month is a puzzle. And while the key to that puzzle may be less believable than the conspiratorial notion that birds are actually government surveillance drones, this absurdity happens to be true.

As American voters were delivering a stinging rebuke to a party seen as putting the interests of wealthy insiders ahead of ordinary Americans, Californians rejected the modest step of imposing a one-time levy on the holdings of individuals with near-unimaginable wealth. Deep-red Texas elected Democrats by stunning margins, but its reliably blue neighbor chose to shield tech moguls from the threat of health care and education spending.

The go-to explanation has been political spending. Billionaires certainly did spend vast amounts to defeat the tax. But opponents of Sherrod Brown heavily outspent supporters as he trounced his Republican opponent. And gleeful critics note that Elon Musk poured money into the campaign of Republican Texas Senate candidate Ken Paxton, only to watch him lose by double digits. Money alone could not turn back this particular blue wave.

Asking why the billionaire tax failed is the wrong question. Instead, consider why California needed it in the first place. The conventional answer focuses on obstacles to a national wealth tax, including valuation and constitutional hurdles. The real problem lies elsewhere, which is how we find ourselves in birds-aren’t-real territory.

The challenges of creating a national wealth tax are clear. The Constitution could demand apportionment — don’t ask — since a wealth tax might stray beyond the protection of the 16th Amendment. Navigating apportionment might be no easier than ratifying a whole new constitutional amendment. 

An anemic federal estate tax raises the question of whether such heroics would even be worth it. That tax raises less than 1 percent of federal revenue each year. Whether a victim of congressional apathy or ruthless planning by the handful of wealthy Americans it targets, it’s hard to imagine that pursuing those same elites while alive would produce better results. 

Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) recently embraced a different approach. Rather than waiting to tax the winners of today’s AI sweepstakes after they have secured their fortunes, Sanders proposed a tax on the companies themselves. His tax on — or rather in — the equity of mammoth AI ventures could unlock an enormous trove of revenues without straying into constitutional minefields or chasing after elusive billionaires. 

Sanders’s revolutionary approach: tax corporations. But don’t we already do that? 

We do, of course. But the corporate tax has a problem not so different than California’s failed tax. Had it been enacted, California’s tax would have invited billionaires to relocate. But corporations can’t escape a federal corporate tax by moving across state lines.

We are told that they can hide their profits overseas. In fact, governments around the world have spent decades and millions upon millions of dollars building a complex system designed to prevent the taxation of the world-spanning corporations that created today’s billionaires. A global tax system, more than half a century after its inception, remains deeply entrenched, incredibly potent and, most importantly, almost entirely unnoticed. 

Beginning in the 1960s, the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development built a vast network of international agreements that has made it difficult for all countries — and, all too predictably, poor countries in particular — to tax multinational corporations. The treaties can reduce or entirely eliminate taxes on profits paid from one country to another, and they forbid taxes on corporations without a “permanent establishment” in a country. Today, more than ever, a business can earn vast profits in a country without offices, warehouses or factories, and pay absolutely no tax there.

We should mourn the California billionaire tax. But we should also take its failure as an invitation to dismantle the hidden mechanism that made it necessary. I would rather tax corporations than their entitled owners anyway.

Google co-founder Sergey Brin personally spent more than $100 million to defeat the billionaire tax. It’s a vast amount for any one person, yet the effort barely left a ripple in his oceanic fortune. Brin’s wealth, although rooted in technology, also owes a debt to abusive tax strategies such as the once-popular double Irish Dutch sandwich. 

That technique — Apple used it as well — would not have been possible without those international agreements. As the name suggests, they eliminated taxes on profits routed through Irish and Dutch subsidiaries of giant tech companies.

If you want to collect the taxes needed to fund urgent priorities like health care and education, that should come as relief as well as a surprise. Rather than dreaming up an entirely new tax, we can simply stop spending millions to protect billionaires from the corporate tax we already have.

Steven Dean, author of “Racial Capitalism and International Tax Law: The Story of Global Jim Crow,” is professor of law and Paul Siskind Research Scholar at Boston University School of Law and serves on the board of the Economic Hardship Reporting Project.

data.title: Nate Silver: Trump could 'absolutely' be removed from office after midterm turmoil
data.description:
Polling analyst Nate Silver suggested there “absolutely” is a chance that President Trump could be removed from office after the GOP and his administration faced clear backlash during the midterms. 

On an episode of the “Still Counting” podcast between Silver and fellow co-hosts Galen Druke and Clare Malone, the pundit asked the pair what prediction markets say about a third Trump impeachment and potential removal ahead of the end of his second term. 

“Are they saying it’s like 25 percent? I have not looked,” Druke said, before Silver called his co-host “uncannily accurate.” 

The pollster, who founded FiveThirtyEight, said it is “entirely reasonable” before Malone rebuffed his assertation, suggesting the president would not get convicted by the upper chamber.

“He could absolutely get removed by the Senate,” Silver said, later adding, “If his approval keeps going down at the rate it is, he’s going to be at whatever, 29 percent, by the end of next year, and like if he’s doing s–t to like profit off selling [Nvidia] chips to China, abso-f—ing-lutely he could be — and he should be.” 

He was referring to the Trump administration’s role in getting Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang reinstated to his post at the chip-making firm. Huang initially stepped down amid revelations that he had affairs with multiple women, including one who had contact with Chinese intelligence.  

Nvidia’s stock drastically rose on Monday morning when the markets closed, though the stock price stumbled downward again later in the week.

Democrats have twice unsuccessfully tried to remove Trump from office, once over whether he directed Ukraine to investigate former President Biden and his family and a second time following the 2020 election and Jan. 6, 2021, Capitol attack.  

Trump was acquitted both times, though seven Senate Republicans joined Democrats during his second trial in voting to convict him.

data.title: Live updates: Bad weather causes Thanksgiving headaches; Trump calls for probe into GDP data
data.description:
Severe weather is upending Thanksgiving plans across the country, with travelers bracing for flight delays and cancellations as a powerful nor’easter moves up the East Coast.

The storm has already pushed back the annual Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade to Saturday and prompted emergency declarations in New York and New Jersey.

President Trump on Thursday also demanded an investigation into revised GDP figures, alleging without evidence that economic growth was deliberately understated ahead of the midterms.

“This is not a small error, this is a massive, and purposeful, error,” Trump wrote on Truth Social.

Meanwhile, federal officials are still monitoring environmental conditions in Iowa after lifting a shelter-in-place order Wednesday night following the Army’s controversial detonation of lead-based explosives. The Trump administration is celebrating the operation’s “success” while casting blame on the Obama administration for the buildup of the toxic materials.

And on Capitol Hill, Sen. Rick Scott (R-Fla.) is headed for a clash with Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) over his push to secure a vote on permanent daylight saving time before year’s end.

Trump is spending Thanksgiving in Florida, where he met Wednesday with NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte amid renewed diplomatic efforts to end Russia’s war in Ukraine.

Follow live below.

data.title: America is back at war, and Americans are still at the mall
data.description:
Earlier this month, on Veterans Day, the nation paused to thank those who have served. In America’s 250th year, the gratitude was genuine: parades, free meals, a handshake in an airport terminal. And then, as it does every November, the moment passed.

Five years ago, as we marked the 20th anniversary of 9/11, I wrote in these pages that a rising number of those who shouldered the burden of two decades of war felt increasingly disconnected from their communities and civilian neighbors. I borrowed a line Tom Nichols captured in The Atlantic, a refrain common among the troops in those early years: “We’re at war. America’s at the mall.”

With American service members once again deployed in combat operations this year, I wish I could report that the line has aged poorly. It hasn’t.

The evidence of the military-civilian divide remains compelling and deeply troubling. The 2025 Reagan National Defense Survey found that just 49 percent of Americans have a great deal of confidence in the military, down 21 points since 2018. Fewer Americans have any personal tie to service at all. Pew Research found that only one-third of adults under 30 had an immediate family member who had served. The Department of Defense and its senior leaders have repeatedly characterized this widening gap as a threat to national security, and the reason is simple: young people rarely aspire to a life they have never seen up close.

The hard truth is that data and awareness without subsequent action are meaningless. For too long we’ve patted ourselves on the back for identifying and giving name to an issue. We’re comfortable getting loud about it for a little while, but when it comes time to take that problem off its pedestal and really put our hands on it, the crowd goes quiet. We are failing, time and again, to put our discussion to work to drive action.

I have spent much of the past three years in working sessions between veterans and their families and employers, college presidents, mayors, installation commanders and service providers.

A few lessons have stood out.

First, the divide is local, and so is the fix. What a transitioning Marine needs in San Diego is not what a Guard family needs in Nashville. National awareness campaigns matter, but the communities making real progress are the ones that stopped waiting for Washington and wrote their own plans: who hires, who trains, who mentors, and how they will measure whether any of it worked.

Second, we have to retire the broken-veteran narrative. When communities see service members, veterans, and military spouses primarily as people to be helped, they design programs. When they see them as students, employees, entrepreneurs, and civic leaders, they design economies. Our goal should be veterans and families who are thriving because of their service, not in spite of it.

Third, thriving is about more than a job. In forum after forum, people described the same pieces: meaningful work, a sense of purpose, a connected community, health and wellness, and the practical tools to navigate a new place. Get one of those right and the others still fail, and the family moves on. Get them right together and families put down roots.

Getting this right is how we inspire the next generation to serve. The most persuasive recruiter in America is not an advertisement, it is a neighbor. When a 16-year-old knows the veteran who owns the HVAC company down the street, the military spouse who teaches her chemistry class, or the Marine who sits on the city council, service becomes a path she can picture for herself.

So here is my ask, in this 250th year. Every member of Congress, mayor, CEO, college president, and installation commander should be able to answer a simple question: what is our community’s plan to make sure those who serve, and their families, thrive here? If the honest answer is a Veterans Day parade, it is time to convene the people who can write a better one, and to invite veterans and military spouses to lead the effort rather than simply be its beneficiaries. If done repeatedly in communities nationwide, these engagements will bridge the civilian-military divide. America doesn’t have to be at the mall. It can be on Main Street.

Kevin M. Schmiegel is a retired Marine Corps lieutenant colonel and co-founder and CEO of ZeroMils.

data.title: Trump, NATO chief urge Russia not to expand war in Ukraine
data.description:
President Trump and NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte urged Russia not to expand its war with Ukraine, as peace talks between the countries have made little headway in recent weeks and as the conflict nears five years. 

Trump and Rutte, following a meeting Wednesday at the president’s Mar-a-Lago resort in Florida, released a joint statement calling their discussion “outstanding” and “very impactful.” The duo said the Russia-Ukraine war and operation in Iran were “the primary subjects,” while they also talked about “all of the record setting achievements that we have made together at the summits in The Hague and at Ankara.” 

“We also discussed the importance of Russia avoiding any actions that intentionally, or unintentionally, expand the war, and the importance of obtaining a peaceful resolution to the war as rapidly as possible,” the pair added. 

The leaders also spoke about increasing defense spending.  

The president, in a Thursday morning post on Truth Social, said he updated Rutte on his discussions with Russian President Vladimir Putin during last week’s summit in China, where he pressed his Putin to “pull back all Military aggression against territories throughout Europe.”

“I really believe this is a strong possibility — Thousands of people are being killed each and every month, A COMPLETE BLOODBATH,” he wrote of the prospects for a peace deal.

Trump, Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping issued a four-point “declaration toward peace” last week, pledging to engage in dialogue on nuclear nonproliferation. The declaration, however, made no mention of the war in Ukraine.

The U.S. mediated peace talks in Abu Dhabi earlier this month between Russia and Ukraine, which resulted in an agreed prisoner swap between the two sides but failed to move the needle toward ending the war itself.  

“Some areas we see places where we can find compromises, others we need to have more discussions, but I think this was a good first step,” Jared Kushner, U.S. special envoy for peace and Trump’s son-in-law, said.

Kushner praised Putin in a recent interview with Axel Springer CEO Mathias Döpfner, saying the Russian leader “has showed restraint,” adding he has “agreed not to use nuclear weapons, which obviously is a big thing.” 

At the same time, both countries have engaged in tit-for-tat strikes.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, meanwhile, has signaled he could turn to congressional Democrats for additional support when they assume control of both chambers in January, should Trump’s diplomatic efforts falter. He has also called for tougher sanctions against Moscow to bring Russia to the negotiating table.

Trump recently urged Zelensky to halt attacks on Russian oil refineries, while Putin reportedly vowed to retaliate against Ukraine over the strikes on its energy infrastructure.

Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha pushed back on Putin’s complaints earlier this week, arguing the Russian leader could put an end to the strikes by ending the war.

“Stop complaining. End the war,” Sybiha wrote in a post on social platform X.
